Drift ≠ Error. DeviationClassification: EXPECTED_ADAPTATION, AUTHORIZED_VARIATION, UNAUTHORIZED_DEVIATION, UNKNOWN.
b_rows_sample.statement: Converts the Chapter-4-derived broken-transmission idea into an engineering drift concept without requiring a universal distance metric, and states Drift ≠ Error (a contextual adaptation may intentionally differ), formalizing a four-value deviation classification; connects this directly to the exception architecture (Rule->Observed deviation->Classification->{Authorized Exception, Expected Contextualization, Unauthorized Deviation}), 'much better than simply PASS/FAIL.'

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'knowledge-drift-model' POSSIBLY relates to 'concept-drift-taxonomy' (batch B0025). Note: A transmission-chain model of knowledge degradation across successive transformations, with a divergence measure D against the authoritative representation and three qualitative regimes (faithful/drifting/governance-intervention); distinct from but conceptually adjacent to the earlier eight-type concept-drift-taxonomy (B0023).

a_rows_sample.anchor: CR-4 FALSIFIED -- TYPE 2, editorial ... 'I would not call it general semantic equivalence ... closer to K1 approx_{Q,Gamma,O} K2 = contextual observational equivalence.' ... [NEG] A naming correction is not a substantive theory blocker. REMOVED.
a_rows_sample.statement: Section 11: falsifies the CR-4 semantic-equivalence multiplicity claim as merely editorial -- the corpus already contains its own correction that the executable CLOSURE-4 tester actually defines a different, narrower relation (approx_obs, contextual observational equivalence K1 approx_{Q,Gamma,O} K2) rather than general semantic equivalence (equiv_sem), already classified in a prior register as 'not conflicting -- mis-slotted'; removed as a blocker.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ⭐⭐ Consequence for my own plan. CR-4 is filed there as ... 'cheapest — the corpus already contains its own repair' and 'nearly self-resolving'. On this evidence it is a three-way conflict in which one option collapses a distinction another was created to protect, and a second carries a standing 'too strong' review. It is not the cheapest of the five conflict records. ... This is the second misclassification found in my own forward plan today
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the investigation's own prior CR-4 disposition (from a previous batch's cr4-equiv-sem-falsified-editorial finding, filed as 'cheapest -- the corpus already contains its own repair', 'nearly self-resolving'): given the newly-found three-way conflict, CR-4 is actually a genuine decision problem where one candidate solution (A) would collapse a distinction another structure (C) was specifically built to protect, and a second candidate (B, CLOSURE-4) carries a standing peer-review verdict of 'too strong' -- so CR-4 is NOT the cheapest of the corpus's five conflict records. Notes CLOSURE-4 is proposed by CR-4 to fill the 'approx_obs' slot while definition A uses an observational criterion to define 'equiv_sem' itself -- two different proposals independently filling different slots of the same 7-tuple with the same kind of content, which is the collapse arriving by two separate routes. Explicitly names this the SECOND misclassification found in the investigator's own forward plan in one day (after D1), noting both errors run the same way: a genuine decision problem filed as cheap/mechanical because its true multiplicity had not yet been enumerated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: x equiv_sem y iff same semantic object under the specified identity semantics. x approx_{Q,Gamma} y iff indistinguishable w.r.t. inquiry Q. x ~_O y iff for all o in O: o(x) equiv_sem o(y). ... The cycle is an artifact of untyped reuse of one symbol, not a genuine circularity.
b_rows_sample.statement: Section 8: restores a typed hierarchy among the three previously conflated relation symbols: x≡_sem y (semantic identity under specified semantics), x≈_{Q,Gamma} y (inquiry/context-relative indistinguishability), x~_O y (congruence: agreement under every operation in O), with ≡_sem⇒≈_{Q,Gamma} and ≡_sem+O⇒congruence_O valid but not the reverse (≈_{Q,Gamma}⇏≡_sem); claims this matches the corpus's own prior finding (CR-4) that the executable tester is ≈_{Q,Gamma,O} not ≡_sem, plus a representation-adequacy result about answering the same questions while differing elsewhere; concludes the apparent ≡⇄≈⇄congruence cycle is an artifact of untyped symbol reuse, broken by stipulating the typing (itself a recorded act).

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'equiv-approx-congruence-typed-hierarchy' POSSIBLY relates to 'cr4-equiv-sem-falsified-editorial' (batch B0067). Note: A restored typed hierarchy among semantic identity, contextual observational equivalence, and operation-congruence, breaking an apparent circularity by typing; related to the CR-4 equiv_sem/approx_obs mis-slotting finding from S2784.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Best action \neq action that merely reduces discrepancy most. An action has cost, risk, reversibility, authority requirements, information value, and consequences.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the naive assumption that the best action is the one that maximally reduces discrepancy: actions carry cost, risk, reversibility, authority requirements, information value, and consequences.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... a^*=\arg\min_a Distance(K_{t+1},I). Why? Because some actions are dangerous; expensive; irreversible; unauthorized; unnecessary; poorly understood. action selection is a decision problem under uncertainty and constraints.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a1*=argmin_a Distance(K_{t+1},I) as insufficient given actions can be dangerous/expensive/irreversible/unauthorized/unnecessary/poorly understood — action selection is a decision problem under uncertainty and constraints.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action is not knowledge ... Knowledge\neq Action and Recommendation\neq Execution. "Changing the firewall rule is likely to solve the discrepancy." That does not mean "Change the firewall rule." There is a governance boundary between those two statements.
a_rows_sample.statement: States Knowledge ≠ Action and Recommendation ≠ Execution as a governance boundary between a diagnostic statement and a directive.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Define an Action ... a=(Intent,Preconditions,Effects,Cost,Risk,Reversibility,Authority,EvidenceRequirements,Context). An action is therefore a structured domain object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Action as a structured domain object a=(Intent,Preconditions,Effects,Cost,Risk,Reversibility,Authority,EvidenceRequirements,Context).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action Preconditions ... Migrate Nexus may require q_1=Backup verified, q_2=Rollback available, q_3=Dependencies identified. Preconditions(a) must be evaluated against K_t. If a critical precondition is unknown Executable(a)=False unless an explicit governance policy permits otherwise.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Preconditions(a) evaluated against K_t (worked with three migration preconditions), with Executable(a)=False by default when a critical precondition is unknown, absent explicit governance override.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action effects ... Transition_a(X_t)\rightarrow X_{t+1} where X is the domain state. But we may not know the exact outcome. X_{t+1} may be probabilistic or uncertain.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines action effects as a (possibly probabilistic/uncertain) domain-state transition Transition_a(X_t)→X_{t+1}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Expected outcome ... o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_m with probabilities P(o_i\mid a,K_t). EU(a) = \sum_i P(o_i\mid a,K_t)U(o_i) where U is the utility function. This is standard expected-utility reasoning.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines standard expected utility EU(a)=Σ_i P(o_i|a,K_t)U(o_i) over possible action outcomes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Information has value ... inspect firewall logs. Its direct operational effect may be \Delta_{operational}=0. But it may greatly reduce uncertainty. Information itself has decision value.
a_rows_sample.statement: States Information itself has decision value, illustrated by an inspection action with zero direct operational effect but high uncertainty reduction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Value of Information ... EVSI(q) = \mathbb E_r[\max_a EU(a\mid K_{t+1}(r))] - \max_a EU(a\mid K_t) where EVSI is the Expected Value of Sample Information. This is a very useful formalization for Lord.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Expected Value of Sample Information EVSI(q)=E_r[max_a EU(a|K_{t+1}(r))]-max_a EU(a|K_t), a formal decision-theoretic value-of-information measure for Lord.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Simpler KnowledgeOS formulation ... VOI(q) = ExpectedDecisionImprovement(q) - Cost(q) as a policy-level approximation. q^* = \arg\max_q VOI(q). Subject to Risk(q)\leq RiskLimit.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a simpler policy-level VOI(q)=ExpectedDecisionImprovement(q)-Cost(q), with q*=argmax_q VOI(q) subject to a risk limit.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This changes the role of Lord ... Generate candidate actions and investigations that have high expected value for reducing relevant uncertainty, discrepancy, or decision risk. Lord: (K_t,I_t,\Delta_t) \rightarrow \mathcal A_t with each candidate annotated by ExpectedBenefit, Cost, Risk, VOI, Reversi
a_rows_sample.statement: Redefines Lord: (K_t,I_t,Δ_t)→A_t, with each candidate action annotated by ExpectedBenefit, Cost, Risk, VOI, and Reversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi is the decision function ... Sārathi: (K_t,I_t,\Delta_t,\mathcal A_t,\rho) \rightarrow Decision ... Decision\in\{Execute,Investigate,Defer,Reject,Escalate,RequestApproval\}. This is important.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines Sārathi:(K_t,I_t,Δ_t,A_t,ρ)→Decision, with Decision∈{Execute,Investigate,Defer,Reject,Escalate,RequestApproval}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi does not have unlimited authority ... production firewall change. Authority(a)=ArchitectureBoard. Therefore Sārathi should produce RequestApproval(a). Not Execute(a). Decision capability\neq Execution authority.
a_rows_sample.statement: States Decision capability ≠ Execution authority, illustrated by a production firewall change requiring Sārathi to produce RequestApproval rather than Execute even when it is the best-evaluated action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision feasibility ... Feasible(a,K_t,\rho) = Preconditions \land Authority \land Constraints \land Safety. Only feasible actions enter the final decision set. \mathcal A^{feasible} \subseteq \mathcal A.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Feasible(a,K_t,ρ)=Preconditions∧Authority∧Constraints∧Safety, filtering the candidate set to A^feasible⊆A before decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Constrained optimization ... a^* = \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A^{feasible}} EU(a) subject to Risk(a)\leq R_{max} and Cost(a)\leq C_{max}. This is already a computationally well-defined problem when the relevant quantities are available.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes constrained action optimization a*=argmax_{a∈A^feasible} EU(a) subject to Risk(a)≤R_max and Cost(a)≤C_max.

a_rows_sample.anchor: But utility is not universal ... There is no universal U(a). For one organization Cost may dominate. For another Safety may dominate. For an incident TimeToRecovery may dominate. UtilityFunction is policy/purpose dependent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues there is no universal utility function U(a); it is policy/purpose dependent (cost-dominant vs safety-dominant vs recovery-time-dominant organizations).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Multi-objective decision making ... Objectives=\{Cost,Risk,Time,Quality,Compliance,Security,Availability\}. There may be no single naturally correct ordering. \mathbf U(a)=(u_1(a),\ldots,u_n(a)). U_\rho(a) = F_\rho(\mathbf U(a)).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a multi-objective utility vector U(a)=(u1(a),...,un(a)) over seven named objectives (Cost/Risk/Time/Quality/Compliance/Security/Availability), aggregated by a policy-specific function F_ρ.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Pareto optimality ... Action a_1 dominates a_2 if u_i(a_1)\geq u_i(a_2) for every criterion i, and strictly better for at least one. The Pareto frontier is \mathcal P = \{a\mid \nexists b:b\succ a\}. Sārathi can present the Pareto-optimal choices to the human decision-maker. This is often better tha
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Pareto dominance and the Pareto frontier P={a|∄b:b≻a}, recommending Sārathi present the Pareto set to a human decision-maker rather than pretend to know exact utility weights.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Inspect logs Low Very Low High Yes ... Change firewall Medium High Low Partly ... Do nothing Zero High None Yes. A naive optimizer might choose DoNothing because Cost=0. A purely discrepancy-driven system might choose ChangeFirewall. A proper decision system may choose InspectLogs becaus
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked five-action decision table (inspect logs/ask owner/run test/change firewall/do nothing) showing a naive cost-minimizer picks DoNothing and a naive discrepancy-minimizer picks ChangeFirewall, while the intended system correctly picks InspectLogs for its high information value at low risk.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Exploration versus exploitation ... Exploration Acquire information a_{explore} ... Exploitation Act on current knowledge a_{exploit} ... Sārathi must balance InformationGain vs ImmediateBenefit. This is closely related to sequential decision theory.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces the exploration (acquire information) vs exploitation (act on current knowledge) tradeoff Sārathi must balance.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
time of observation 
eq time of validity 
eq time of belief 
eq time of decision 
eq time of event ... "Nexus is version 3.69" without being able to answer: When was that true? When did we know it? When did we decide it? When did the system actually change?
b_rows_sample.statement: States five distinct time axes must never be conflated: observation, validity, belief, decision, and event time — otherwise KnowledgeOS cannot answer when a fact was true, known, decided, or when the underlying system actually changed.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Time is not one dimension ... Valid time T_v(A) ... Observation time T_o(A) ... Knowledge time T_k(A) ... Decision time T_d(A) ... Event time T_e(A) ... T_e
eq T_o
eq T_k
eq T_d and none should be silently substituted for another. ... Example ... Nexus server was upgraded on 2026-08-20. Engineer
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines five formal time axes (T_v,T_o,T_k,T_d,T_e) worked with a concrete four-date upgrade/discovery/ingestion/decision timeline.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assertion temporal structure ... A=(P,E,\Sigma,\Pi,T_v,T_o,T_k,Context,ID). Decision time normally belongs to the Decision event, rather than the assertion itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the assertion structure to A=(P,E,Σ,Π,T_v,T_o,T_k,Context,ID), noting decision time belongs to a separate Decision event, not the assertion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Valid time is usually an interval ... T_v=[t_{start},t_{end}) ... known start; unknown start; known end; unknown end. T_v=[2026-08-20,\infty). ... Unknown temporal boundaries ... T_v=(?,2026-08-25]. Unknown temporal boundary\neq false.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines valid time as an interval T_v=[t_start,t_end) potentially with open/unknown bounds on either side, requiring KnowledgeOS represent unknown boundaries rather than treat them as false.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Event time ... Nexus was upgraded ... e=Upgrade(Nexus,3.69,3.70) ... occurrence time T_e(e). The resulting state Version(Nexus)=3.70 has a validity interval. Event\neq State. ... State transition ... X_{t+1} = \delta_X(X_t,e_t). This is different from the Knowledge State K_{t+1}=\delta_K(K_t,o_t). W
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes an Event (with occurrence time T_e) from the resulting State (with a validity interval) — Event ≠ State — and defines a domain-state transition X_{t+1}=δ_X(X_t,e_t) distinct from the Knowledge State transition K_{t+1}=δ_K(K_t,o_t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: World state versus Knowledge State ... World/domain state X_t represents the state of the domain/reality being modeled. Knowledge state K_t represents what KnowledgeOS knows/believes/accepts about that domain. X_t\neq K_t. KnowledgeOS can be wrong about the world.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the central Step 16 result X_t ≠ K_t: the world/domain state and KnowledgeOS's knowledge of it are distinct, so KnowledgeOS can be wrong about the world.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The epistemic gap ... X_t: Version(Nexus)=3.72 but K_t: Version(Nexus)=3.69. K_t\neq X_t. KnowledgeOS may not know the discrepancy exists. A knowledge system cannot detect an unknown discrepancy without some new evidence or observation. That should be explicitly accepted in our theory.
b_rows_sample.statement: States a fundamental limitation: a knowledge system cannot detect an unknown discrepancy without new evidence, illustrated by a world/knowledge version mismatch KnowledgeOS is unaware of.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Event sourcing perspective ... NexusProvisioned, NexusConfigured, NexusUpgraded, FirewallChanged, CertificateRenewed, BackupTested ... X_t=Fold(X_0,e_1,\ldots,e_n). X_t=Fold(\delta_X,X_0,H_X) where H_X=(e_1,\ldots,e_n). This is very compatible with event-sourced architecture. ... Knowledge evolution
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines two parallel event-sourced folds: domain state X_t=Fold(δ_X,X_0,H_X) over a domain event vocabulary (Provisioned/Configured/Upgraded/etc.), and Knowledge state K_t=Fold(δ_K,K_0,H_K) over a knowledge event vocabulary (AssertionCreated/EvidenceAdded/ConflictDetected/etc.).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Two histories ... H_X = domain/world event history and H_K = KnowledgeOS epistemic history. They are related but not identical. World: Nexus upgraded ↓ KnowledgeOS: did not know ↓ Engineer observes ↓ KnowledgeOS learns. So H_X contains the upgrade before H_K contains knowledge of the upgrade. ... Th
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes domain history H_X from knowledge history H_K (an event enters H_X before knowledge of it enters H_K), allowing EventOccurred to be represented without KnowledgeOfEvent — reality does not wait for observation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge lag ... L(A)=T_k(A)-T_e(A) ... This is the knowledge lag. L=6 days. This can itself become an operational metric.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Knowledge lag L(A)=T_k(A)-T_e(A) as a candidate operational metric.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Staleness ... Age(A)=Now-T_{lastVerified}(A). Age\neq Staleness. Staleness depends on how rapidly the underlying fact can change. ... Volatility ... Software version Medium ... IP address High ... PhD degree Very Low ... Current CPU load Extremely High ... a 30-day-old assertion about CPU load is us
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Age(A) and distinguishes it from Staleness=f(Age,Volatility,Context), worked with a Volatility table (software version/IP/hostname/degree/architecture principle/CPU load) showing identical age can mean very different staleness.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal validity is policy-dependent ... ValidUntil defined by explicit source; domain rule; expiry date; observation policy; volatility policy. TemporalValidity is partly epistemic and partly policy-governed.
b_rows_sample.statement: States TemporalValidity is partly epistemic and partly policy-governed, with ValidUntil determined by explicit source, domain rule, expiry date, or volatility policy.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal conflict ... T_v(P_1)=[2025,2026-08-20) and T_v(P_2)=[2026-08-20,\infty). Then P_1 and P_2 are not contradictory. They describe different temporal states. Conflict(P_1,P_2) requires temporal compatibility. ... Overlapping contradictory intervals ... P_1 valid [2026-08-01,2026-09-01) and P_2
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines conflict detection to require temporally overlapping validity intervals (non-overlapping successive intervals are not contradictory), introducing a specific TemporalConflict classification identifying the overlapping sub-interval rather than a bare Conflict=True.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Bitemporal knowledge ... Valid time ... Transaction/knowledge time ... BitemporalKnowledge can represent (T_v,T_k). ... Why bitemporality matters ... What did KnowledgeOS believe on August 24? We must not answer using today's knowledge. We need K_{2026-08-24} not K_{now}. This is crucial for auditin
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Bitemporal knowledge (valid time × knowledge time), required so a question like 'what did KnowledgeOS believe on a past date' is answered from the historical knowledge state, not today's.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Historical reconstruction ... K(t)=Fold(\delta_K,K_0,H_K^{\leq t}). This gives us temporal knowledge replay. ... Decision reconstruction ... DecisionBasis(D_{27}) \subseteq K_{27}. We must not retrospectively use knowledge learned on August 28 to justify a decision made August 27. No retroactive epi
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines historical knowledge replay K(t)=Fold(δ_K,K_0,H_K^{≤t}), used to constrain DecisionBasis(D)⊆K_t at decision time, establishing the major invariant of no retroactive epistemic contamination.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge version ... KV_t as a version/snapshot of the Knowledge State. K-2026-08-27-0042 containing assertions; entity identities; conflicts; accepted conclusions; policies; ontology version; provenance. ... But a version is not the same as time ... Version(K) is an identifier. Time(K) is temporal
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a Knowledge Version KV_t as a full snapshot (assertions, entities, conflicts, conclusions, policies, ontology version, provenance), distinguishing Version (identifier) from Timestamp (temporal metadata) — Version ≠ Timestamp.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Event versus snapshot ... An event says: Something changed. A snapshot says: This is the resulting state at a particular point. Event\neq Snapshot. We should preserve both. ... Event structure ... e=(EventID,Type,AggregateID,Payload,Actor,OccurredAt,RecordedAt,Provenance,CorrelationID). ... Event ti
b_rows_sample.statement: States Event ≠ Snapshot (both must be preserved), defines an Event structure e=(EventID,Type,AggregateID,Payload,Actor,OccurredAt,RecordedAt,Provenance,CorrelationID), and reaffirms OccurredAt ≠ RecordedAt with a firewall-change example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge events ... EvidenceObserved, AssertionCreated, AssertionUpdated, AssertionRetracted, ConflictDetected, ResolutionCompleted, EntityResolved, EntityMerged, KnowledgeCommitted. Each becomes part of H_K.
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists nine named knowledge-event types feeding H_K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retraction ... Retract(A) creates a new epistemic event. The historical fact that KnowledgeOS once held A remains. This is essential for auditability. ... Revision ... Supersedes(A_2,A_1). The old assertion remains historically visible. Revision preserves history.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Retract(A) creates a new event without erasing the historical fact of holding A, and Revision via Supersedes(A2,A1) preserves the superseded assertion's historical visibility.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge lineage ... Source ↓ Observation ↓ Assertion ↓ Assessment ↓ Acceptance ↓ Decision ↓ Action ↓ Outcome ↓ New Observation. Each node has temporal semantics. This creates a complete epistemic lineage.
b_rows_sample.statement: Assembles a complete epistemic-lineage chain (Source→Observation→Assertion→Assessment→Acceptance→Decision→Action→Outcome→New Observation), each node carrying its own temporal semantics.

a_notations: Sarathi: Lord's selected action -> actual behavior
a_aliases: Step 15: Decision Theory, Value of Information, Action Selection, and Sārathi
b_aliases: Step 16: Temporal Knowledge, Events, State Evolution, and Knowledge Versioning

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'temporal-knowledge-state-evolution-versioning' POSSIBLY relates to 'decision-theory-action-selection-sarathi' (batch B0021). Note: S0872's Step 16: five separated time axes; refined bitemporal assertion structure; World-state X_t vs Knowledge-state K_t as parallel, only Obs-connected state machines (the epistemic observation boundary); knowledge lag and volatility-dependent staleness; historical replay with no-retroactive-contamination; Allen-style interval relations; prediction lifecycle; time-aware Zero/Lord/Sarathi; temporal versioning of policy/ontology/rules for reproducibility; T1-T15 invariants; hands off to Step 17 (ontology/concepts/semantics/domain models).

a_rows_sample.anchor: O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t ... Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the full research pipeline O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t (observation, conditional evidence assessment, conditional reasoning, determination, fact), identifying D_t as the determination and concluding that Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework, since the prior pipeline treated Observation->Evidence->Fact as deterministic rather than making each stage explicitly conditional on context/time/model/rules/assumptions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(F\mid O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) where A_t represents assumptions. This is not a recommendation that the Kernel should store this probability. It is a research question about what the probabilistic regime needs.
a_rows_sample.statement: The framework's P(F|O) is too simplistic because the same observation can support different propositions depending on context, interpretation, prior facts, model, measurement method, source reliability, time, and assumptions; proposes P(F|O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) instead, explicitly framed as a research question about probabilistic-regime requirements, not a Kernel storage recommendation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: certainty of the rule != certainty of its premises != certainty of the conclusion. This is precisely the combination problem that the framework identifies but hasn't yet solved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the framework's use of the word 'established' for facts feeding logic/rules: a fact can have a graded epistemic state (e.g. P(F1)=0.8) even while the logical rule F1 and F2 => K applying to it is completely valid; therefore certainty of the rule, certainty of its premises, and certainty of the conclusion are three distinct things -- this is the combination problem the framework identifies but has not yet solved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Layer 1 -- uncertainty in extraction: O -> F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8. Layer 2 -- uncertainty propagated through reasoning: given P(F1)=0.8 and F1=>K, we need to determine the epistemic state of K. ... How does uncertainty in premises interact with logical structure?
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies two distinct uncertainty layers: Layer 1, uncertainty in extraction (O->F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8), and Layer 2, uncertainty propagated through reasoning (given P(F1)=0.8 and a rule F1=>K, the epistemic state of K is not automatically P(K)=0.8 and requires a combination semantics); the real underlying problem is how uncertainty in premises interacts with logical structure -- more fundamental than choosing among Bayesian/fuzzy/Dempster-Shafer.

a_rows_sample.anchor: uncertainty representation; conditional structure; combination rule; temporal aspect; conflict handling; ignorance representation. I would not call these invariants. They are dimensions along which the frameworks differ. ... We need a stricter definition of invariant: I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the framework's list of cross-framework commonalities (uncertainty representation, conditional structure, combination rule, temporal aspect, conflict handling, ignorance representation) being called 'invariants': since Bayesian != Dempster-Shafer != Fuzzy != Argumentation in their uncertainty semantics, 'all frameworks represent uncertainty' establishes only a common research concern, not a mathematical invariant. Proposes the stricter test: an invariant must satisfy I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: There may be a common algebraic structure underlying all these frameworks, e.g. lattice or measure-theoretic structure. I would mark this highly speculative. ... P(p) and mu(p) and mu_fuzzy(p) and Acceptable(p) may not be representations of one common mathematical object. They could represent different epistemic properties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Marks the framework's proposed 'common algebraic structure' (e.g. a lattice or measure-theoretic structure unifying all evidence-combination frameworks) as highly speculative and premature: before seeking a common algebra one must establish that the objects being represented (P(p), mu(p), mu_fuzzy(p), Acceptable(p)) are actually the same kind of thing -- they could instead represent different epistemic properties, which is exactly the danger the research has been trying to avoid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: First: What is the epistemic object? Second: What is the determination operation? Third: What does each regime represent? Fourth: When can two representations be considered equivalent? Fifth: What survives those equivalences? Only then do we ask: What is invariant?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a safer six-step research ordering before asking about invariance: first, what is the epistemic object; second, what is the determination operation; third, what does each regime represent; fourth, when can two representations be considered equivalent; fifth, what survives those equivalences; only then, what is invariant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_t(p)=(proposition, support, justification, status, uncertainty, time). ... Bayesian theory may primarily represent uncertainty. Argumentation represents support/attack. Non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status. Epistemic logic represents knowledge relations. Temporal logic represents temporal truth. Measurement theory represents numerical attributes. These may be different dimensions of an epistemic state, rather than competing representations of one scalar object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Hypothesizes that epistemic state itself needs decomposition rather than being a generic scalar output E in script-E: E_t(p)=(proposition,support,justification,status,uncertainty,time). Under this hypothesis, different mathematical frameworks may each be capturing a different DIMENSION of epistemic state rather than competing representations of one scalar object: Bayesian theory primarily represents uncertainty, argumentation represents support/attack, non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status, epistemic logic represents knowledge relations, temporal logic represents temporal truth, and measurement theory represents numerical attributes. Explicitly framed as a hypothesis needing testing, not a proposed Kernel model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: How should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state? I would retain that. But add: What are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced? And then: Which components are regime-specific and which are regime-independent?
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the central research question: retains 'how should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state', and adds two further questions -- what are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced, and which components are regime-specific versus regime-independent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Is Knowledge probabilistic? No. Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic? Some extraction processes are probabilistic. Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic? It can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent. ... What exactly is being represented by the probability?
a_rows_sample.statement: Traces the evolving answer to a recurring question across the discussion: 'Is Knowledge probabilistic?' -> No; 'Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic?' -> some extraction processes are; 'Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic?' -> it can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent; the deeper open question that now emerges is 'What exactly is being represented by the probability?'

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is observed? -> Observation. What makes it evidence? -> Evidence relation. ... What does probability represent? -> Unknown -- investigate. ... Are these actually different lenses on one epistemic state, or are they lenses on different dimensions of it?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes replacing an immediate 11-framework comparison with a 16-row question/research-target matrix (what is observed->Observation; what makes it evidence->Evidence relation; evidence for what->Proposition/hypothesis; what makes a proposition determined->Determination; what makes determination legitimate->Reasoning/justification; what can be uncertain->Observation/proposition/model/inference; what can be revised->Determination/conclusion/state; what does time change->Validity/evidence/state; what does probability represent->Unknown, investigate; what does logic represent->Inference structure; what does argumentation represent->Support/attack; what does fuzzy value represent->Truth/vagueness; what does D-S represent->Evidence/ignorance; what does epistemic logic represent->Knowledge relation; what does temporal logic represent->Temporal properties; what does measurement theory represent->Empirical-to-numerical representation), then asks whether these are different lenses on one epistemic state or lenses on different dimensions of it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Strong: correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison. Needs correction: P(F|O) is too simplistic; "established facts" should not automatically be treated as deterministic; the listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives an explicit verdict on the uploaded framework document: five strong points (correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison) and six points needing correction (P(F|O) too simplistic; 'established facts' should not automatically be treated as deterministic; listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object). Also explicitly agrees with the framework's constraint: 'Do not design the Kernel. Do not change its boundary. Challenge the architecture; do not become its architect.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: (O, E, F_{<t}, C, R) -> D_t(p) where D_t(p) is the determination of proposition p at time t. Then we investigate how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. I think that is the next missing piece before we can responsibly talk about the invariant.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes continuing research at exactly one point: formalizing '(O,E,F_{<t},C,R) -> D_t(p)' as the operation producing the determination of proposition p at time t, then investigating how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. -- framed as the next missing piece before responsibly discussing invariance.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and it must be able to explain and revise that determination later. ... Information -> What did we actually observe? -> ... -> What can we defend as "knowledge"?
a_rows_sample.statement: States the business problem in one sentence: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and must be able to explain and revise that determination later; there is no direct pipeline from information to knowledge -- it passes through what was observed, what the observation means, what evidence it provides, evidence strength, existing facts/evidence, applicable rules, conflicts, current conclusion, and finally what can be defended as knowledge, with every step conditional and imperfect.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Port 8081 is open. That's an observation. Does it prove Nexus is available? No. It is evidence supporting that possibility. ... another process uses the port; the service is running but inaccessible from the required network; the information is outdated; this is not the production server. So: Observation != Evidence != Fact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 1 (Information is not automatically evidence): 'Port 8081 is open' is an observation, not proof that Nexus is available -- it is evidence supporting that possibility only, since alternative explanations exist (another process on the port, network-inaccessible service, outdated information, wrong server); therefore Observation != Evidence != Fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Observation A -> supports "Nexus is running"; Observation B -> supports "Nexus is reachable"; Observation C -> contradicts "Nexus is reachable from production". Now what? We have conflicting evidence. The system must determine: What should we currently conclude? This is the determination problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 2 (evidence does not automatically create a fact): three observations produce conflicting evidence (A supports 'Nexus is running', B supports 'Nexus is reachable', C contradicts 'Nexus is reachable from production'); the system must determine what to currently conclude -- this is the determination problem.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A system is "migration ready" only if: dependencies are identified; network access is verified; backup is verified; certificates are understood; rollback is defined. ... Dependencies: Strong, Network: Strong, Backup: Uncertain, Certificates: Missing, Rollback: Strong. Can we say "Migration ready"? Not simply by looking at the data. We need the rule for determining readiness.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 3 (the rules for determining something matter): given a five-criterion migration-readiness policy (dependencies/network/backup/certificates/rollback) and mixed evidence strength per criterion (Strong/Strong/Uncertain/Missing/Strong), whether 'migration ready' can be asserted cannot be read off the data alone -- an explicit rule for determining readiness is required.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Architect A says: "80% confidence is sufficient. Proceed." Architect B says: "The certificate dependency is unknown. Therefore readiness cannot be established." Both have the same information. But they use different reasoning criteria. ... KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct. It should preserve enough information so that the appropriate reasoning regime can make its determination.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 4 (different reasoning methods can produce different answers): two architects viewing identical evidence reach opposite conclusions (Architect A: '80% confidence is sufficient, proceed' vs Architect B: 'certificate dependency unknown, therefore readiness cannot be established') because they apply different reasoning criteria (Bayesian probability vs logical derivation vs argumentation vs Dempster-Shafer belief+ignorance vs non-monotonic defeasible conclusions); principle derived: KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct, but should preserve enough information for the appropriate reasoning regime to make its own determination.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We don't yet know what "knowledge" actually is ... Is a highly probable conclusion knowledge? Is a logically derived conclusion knowledge? Is an institutionally approved statement knowledge? Is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true? Is an old fact still knowledge after it becomes obsolete? Is "unknown" itself part of knowledge? These are not implementation questions yet. They are domain-definition questions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 6 (we don't yet know what 'knowledge' actually is), the deepest of the six: facts, evidence, observations, justification, reasoning, probability, belief, commitments, conclusions, and knowledge have not yet had their boundaries rigorously established; poses six unresolved domain-definition questions (is a highly probable conclusion knowledge; is a logically derived conclusion knowledge; is an institutionally approved statement knowledge; is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true; is an old, obsolete fact still knowledge; is 'unknown' itself part of knowledge) -- explicitly framed as domain-definition questions, not implementation questions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Information -> Evidence -> Reasoning -> Determination -> Knowledge ... contextual; time-dependent; incomplete; sometimes probabilistic; sometimes logical; sometimes argumentative; sometimes governed by explicit rules.
a_rows_sample.statement: Summarizes the business problem as a transformation from Information to Defensible Knowledge via Information->Evidence->Reasoning->Determination->Knowledge, where the transformation is contextual, time-dependent, incomplete, and sometimes probabilistic, logical, argumentative, or governed by explicit rules.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Of 10 propositions the corpus itself requires, {n_ok} are cleanly expressible. THREE are inexpressible (negation, conditional, quantification), TWO are lossy (validity interval, unit), ONE is not a proposition at all in this type system, and ONE is ambiguous between a value and an epistemic marker.
b_rows_sample.statement: Classifies ten corpus-sourced natural-language propositions against P=(Entity,Dimension,Value): 'Nexus.version=3.69' EXPRESSIBLE; 'Nexus.version=3.69 in production context' EXPRESSIBLE-VIA-A but shown to make context-varying propositions distinct assertions rather than distinct propositions; 'Alice is Board chair from date to date' LOSSY (drops which board and the validity interval, since A's single t is assertion-time not valid-time, per Step 185's T_valid != T_known distinction); 'a1 contradicts a2' NOT-A-PROPOSITION (expressed via an R-edge, leaving two content mechanisms P and R with no stated relationship); 'NOT Nexus.version=3.69' INEXPRESSIBLE (no negation, would require negative values in V_D which Step 264 does not provide); 'IF v>=3.60 THEN patch-current' INEXPRESSIBLE (no conditional -- the exact conditional-determination problem the corpus opened with on 2026-08-25); 'EVERY committee has >=3 members' INEXPRESSIBLE (no quantification/arithmetic over a population); 'Nexus is ready to be migrated' EXPRESSIBLE-BUT-EMPTY (holds the conclusion but not the deriving rule, which lives in the class-C, no-decision-procedure Policy); 'response time = 250ms' LOSSY (drops the unit, Step 264.14's own 'another layer' that is not placed in V); 'Nexus.version is UNKNOWN' AMBIGUOUS (either an epistemic marker inside the value space -- a category error Step 264 warns against -- or indistinguishable assertion-absence).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The object the corpus named as MISSING on day 1 -- Determination -- is still missing on day 6, and the terminal proposition type cannot express the conditional structure that Determination was introduced to carry. The theory closed around the part of the problem it could formalize.
b_rows_sample.statement: EXP-20 checks the terminal type P=(Entity,Dimension,Value)/K=(A,R) (closed 2026-08-30) against the corpus's own founding research question, opened 2026-08-25/26 as 'what substrate must be preserved so multiple determination regimes can independently reconstruct the same phenomenon' and 'Determination is the missing mathematical object'; finds the conditional determination example remains INEXPRESSIBLE (per EXP-19), its deriving rule lives in Policy (class-C, no decision procedure per Step 266 s266.22/s266.23), and a grep for 'Determination' across Steps 258-270's K or A definitions returns nothing -- Determination as a named object is entirely absent from the terminal model six days after being identified as the founding gap; concludes the theory closed around the part of the problem it could formalize.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The object the corpus named as the missing mathematical object on day 1 is absent from every terminal artefact on day 6, and the terminal proposition type cannot express the conditional structure it was introduced to carry. This is the single most consequential finding in this document. ... the theory closed around the part of the problem it could formalize, and the reader of the terminal steps cannot tell, because no terminal step records that the founding question was dropped.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finding CS-4 (called the single most consequential finding in the document): the corpus opened (2026-08-25 23:57-00:03) on the conditional determination problem ('What substrate must be preserved so multiple determination regimes can independently reconstruct the same phenomenon?', and 'Determination is the missing mathematical object'), but closed on P=(E,D,V) and K=(A,R); a grep across the six terminal steps (262-267) finds zero occurrences of 'Determination'; the conditional example IF version>=3.60 THEN patch-current remains inexpressible, and its deriving rule lives in class-C (no decision procedure) Policy; explicitly warns that no terminal step records that the founding question was silently dropped, so a reader of only the terminal artifacts cannot detect the abandonment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: "Assertions from authority: generated may not be authoritative without human review" is a real, running EKP rule ... It is a proposition about assertions with a quantifier and a modal. Inexpressible (CS-4).
b_rows_sample.statement: A third worked counterexample: a real, currently-enforced EKP rule ('assertions from authority:generated may not be authoritative without human review', per the Knowledge-Constitution's AI-collaboration principles) is a proposition about assertions carrying a quantifier and a modal, and is inexpressible in the terminal proposition type -- alongside two other counterexamples: identity underdetermination (A-in-K disagreeing on 2 of 3 probes across four equalities) and an unbacked contradicts-relation that cannot itself carry evidence/provenance/status.

a_rows_sample.anchor: information is not the same thing as meaning. ... information can exist objectively in the relationships between events before interpretation, while meaning is something that develops through systems capable of exploiting that information. ... EVENT/STATE -> INFORMATION -> CODING/REPRESENTATION -> MEANING -> BELIEF -> KNOWLEDGE.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports Dretske's central distinction information != meaning (information exists objectively in relationships between events prior to interpretation; meaning develops through systems capable of exploiting it), formalized as Event/State->Information->Coding/Representation->Meaning->Belief->Knowledge, replacing a simpler word->meaning->knowledge chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: information as a reduction/elimination of possibilities. His simple example reduces eight possible candidates to one, producing 3 bits of information. ... POSSIBILITY SPACE -> [observation/signal] -> REDUCED POSSIBILITY SPACE -> INFORMATION. This is potentially more fundamental than our current concept of "knowledge item." ... A signal carries the information that s is F when, given the signal and relevant background knowledge, the conditional probability of s being F is 1, whereas given the background knowledge alone it is less than 1.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports Dretske's information-theoretic foundation treating information as reduction of a possibility space (eight candidates reduced to one yields 3 bits), proposed as potentially more fundamental than 'knowledge item'; formalizes his semantic-information definition: a signal carries the information that s is F when P(s is F | signal, background) = 1 while P(s is F | background alone) < 1, flagged as directly relevant to the project's truth/evidence/observation/assurance work.

type_signature.codomain: conditional probability of s being F

a_rows_sample.anchor: the same amount of information can be represented by very different codes ... Words and sentences are representations. They are not the fundamental knowledge objects. Dretske gives us very strong support for that conclusion.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports Dretske's separation of information from the representation/code carrying it (the same information can be encoded longer/shorter/redundant), reinforcing the KNOWLEDGE DOMAIN (fact/proposition/information/evidence/relation) vs REPRESENTATION LAYER (words/sentences/documents/diagrams/code/embeddings) separation and the conclusion that words/sentences are representations, not fundamental knowledge objects.

a_rows_sample.anchor: checking whether the instrument itself is reliable is a different informational operation. During calibration, the instrument temporarily becomes the object of investigation rather than simply the channel. ... knowledge about the domain; knowledge about the evidence source; knowledge about the reliability of the observation mechanism.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses Dretske's calibration example (a measuring instrument transmits information about a measured system, but checking the instrument's own reliability is a distinct informational operation where the instrument temporarily becomes the object of investigation) to derive three distinct knowledge types KnowledgeOS must separate: knowledge about the domain, knowledge about the evidence source, and knowledge about the reliability of the observation mechanism, with a parallel Channel->Calibration->Channel Reliability path alongside Source->Channel->Observation->Evidence->Information->Belief->Knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Dretske instead develops: information -> information-caused belief -> knowledge. He explicitly proposes an information-theoretic replacement for the traditional justified-true-belief account. ... a particularly subtle distinction between information causing a belief and information causally sustaining a belief. ... OBSERVATION -> INFORMATION ACQUISITION -> BELIEF FORMATION -> BELIEF SUSTENANCE -> KNOWLEDGE CLAIM.
a_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts Floridi's semantic-information->relevance->account->knowledge route with Dretske's information->information-caused-belief->knowledge route (an information-theoretic replacement for justified-true-belief), distinguishing information causing a belief from information causally sustaining it, proposing a five-stage pipeline Observation->Information Acquisition->Belief Formation->Belief Sustenance->Knowledge Claim instead of treating evidence as a static attachment to a claim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: nested informational shells. A structure may carry information that t is a square while that information is nested inside information about another object, which may itself be nested inside something else. ... knowledge depth may not simply be graph distance. It may involve informational containment/specificity/dependency.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports Dretske's Chapter-7 'nested informational shells' (information about one thing can be nested inside information about another, recursively), proposing this refines the project's 'knowledge depth' problem: depth may not be graph distance but informational containment/specificity/dependency.

a_rows_sample.anchor: information carried by a semantic structure cannot be false, while beliefs can be false. Therefore: INFORMATION ≠ BELIEF ≠ KNOWLEDGE. ... Dretske explicitly distinguishes the concept from a particular belief: structure types have meaning, while tokens can have truth value.
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives Information != Belief != Knowledge from Dretske's point that information (as he defines it) cannot be false while beliefs can, and separately distinguishes concept (a structure type, carrying meaning) from a particular belief (a token, carrying truth value) -- flagged as crucial for the Kernel.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a system's semantic content can remain the same even when its physical realization differs; two physically different structures can have the same semantic content. ... KnowledgeOS should be representation-independent. The Kernel should not care whether knowledge is represented as JSON, SQL, Markdown, PDF, graph, vector, sentence, code, database record, AI context. What matters is the informational/semantic structure being represented.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses Dretske's multiple-realizability point (same semantic content, different physical realizations) to state a representation-independence principle: the Kernel must not care whether knowledge is represented as JSON/SQL/Markdown/PDF/graph/vector/sentence/code/database-record/AI-context -- only the informational/semantic structure matters.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Floridi and Dretske are converging on some things but disagreeing or emphasizing different layers on others. That is precisely what we need from the Zero Lens. ... I would not freeze the Kernel yet. The next useful step is to construct a Floridi × Dretske comparative matrix and derive only the invariants that survive both books.
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes Floridi and Dretske converge on some points and diverge/emphasize different layers on others, which is exactly the intended use of the Zero Lens; explicitly declines to freeze the Kernel, proposing a Floridi x Dretske comparative matrix to derive only the invariants surviving both books as the next research step.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Floridi gives us the idea that a representation is made at a selected **Level of Abstraction**, with a selected set of observables.
a_rows_sample.statement: Ties the Knowledge Capacity construct back to all four prior book-lenses: Floridi's Level-of-Abstraction/observables defines what portion of a system can be represented; Gärdenfors' epistemic state contains commitments and changes through inputs/expansion/revision/contraction; Dretske separates information from its physical/linguistic encoding, so the capacity to 'write' information is not identical to the information itself; Searle adds that some information participates in institutional structures where context determines what something counts as.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 95.19 — Information-flow policy ... Label(K) as confidentiality classification. Flow(K_1,K_2) only if PermittedFlow(Label(K_1),Label(K_2)).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines information-flow policy: Flow(K_1,K_2) requires PermittedFlow(Label(K_1),Label(K_2)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: semantic information → knowledge → reality ... semantic information as well-formed, meaningful, truthful data ... knowledge is relevant semantic information that is properly accounted for. ... SYSTEM/DOMAIN -> LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION -> {observables,behaviour,relations} -> DATA -[meaning]-> INFORMATION -[truth]-> SEMANTIC INFORMATION -[relevance]-> KNOWLEDGE -[account]-> WELL-FOUNDED KNOWLEDGE.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports Floridi's central chain semantic-information->knowledge->reality, defining semantic information as well-formed/meaningful/truthful data and knowledge as relevant semantic information properly accounted for, formalized as a full pipeline from System/Domain through Level of Abstraction (observables/behaviour/relations) to Data, Information (via meaning), Semantic Information (via truth), Knowledge (via relevance), and Well-Founded Knowledge (via account); concludes Knowledge Space should be modeled as a structured space of informational descriptions at different abstraction levels, not a collection of knowledge objects.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Words and sentences should almost certainly NOT be Kernel primitives of Knowledge itself. They belong to a representation / expression layer.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the idea that 'knowledge can be expressed in words' implies words/sentences are Kernel primitives: Floridi treats informational content as not identical with its particular encoding (books/databases/websites/words/sentences all carry information without being it), so the chain Word->Sentence->Proposition->Semantic Content is not Word=Knowledge; words and sentences belong to a representation/expression layer, one of the file's first recorded architectural conclusions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Level of Abstraction is a finite non-empty set of observables. ... A Knowledge Space boundary should normally be a boundary of abstraction, purpose, scope and observability. ... The object did not change. The Knowledge Space changed because the Level of Abstraction changed.
b_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Floridi's Level of Abstraction (LoA, a finite non-empty set of observables -- an observable being an interpreted typed variable representing a system feature, where 'system' can be physical/conceptual/mathematical/moral) as the answer to 'should a topic have a boundary?': yes, but as a boundary of abstraction/purpose/scope/observability, not an ontological one; illustrated by 'Car' described completely differently across four LoAs (brand/model/year; engine/transmission/fuel; combustion/thermodynamics/materials; molecular structure/quantum phenomena) where the object is unchanged but the Knowledge Space differs by LoA -- called the single most valuable idea in the book for KnowledgeOS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Knowledge Space is potentially unbounded in extension, but every usable knowledge representation is bounded by a selected Level of Abstraction, purpose, context and scope.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the project's 'knowledge can be infinite if you go deeper and deeper' intuition into: Knowledge Space is potentially unbounded in extension, but every usable knowledge representation is bounded by a selected LoA, purpose, context and scope, citing Floridi's Gradient of Abstraction allowing movement across LoA views.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the behaviour of the system at that LoA ... SCOPE BOUNDARY, SEMANTIC BOUNDARY, VALIDITY/BEHAVIOURAL BOUNDARY ... If you observe chess only by files, you cannot reconstruct the full game. If you observe it only by ranks, you also cannot. But when the two views are combined, the underlying game becomes recoverable. ... A topic does NOT necessarily need one boundary. ... KnowledgeOS should probably support overlapping knowledge spaces rather than forcing a single tree of topics.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses Floridi's 'behaviour' (allowed observable-value combinations at a LoA, defined by a predicate) to distinguish Scope/Semantic/Validity-Behavioural boundaries (illustrated by an Election topic where not every voter/candidate/ballot relationship is valid); uses the chess files/ranks example (neither view alone reconstructs the game, combined they do) to argue a topic need not have one boundary but can be a projection into a knowledge space, concluding KnowledgeOS should support overlapping knowledge spaces rather than a single topic tree -- a major architectural consequence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: data exists, data is well-formed, the well-formed data is meaningful, the meaning is truthful. ... "Purple elephants negotiate database treaties." ... false information is not semantic information in the strict sense, but pseudo-information/misinformation. ... Claim: syntactic_status, semantic_status, truth_status, relevance_status, evidential_status, account_status.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports Floridi's four-condition definition of semantic information (data exists, is well-formed, is meaningful, is truthful) and his claim that false information is pseudo-information/misinformation rather than semantic information proper; illustrated by 'purple elephants negotiate database treaties' being syntactically valid but questionable on meaningful/truthful/relevant/knowledge; proposes replacing a single truth=true/false flag with a Claim record carrying six independent status fields (syntactic, semantic, truth, relevance, evidential, account).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Network Theory of Account ... a piece of semantic information is an answer to a question, but that answer generates further questions. ... How come?/historical, What for?/teleological, How does it work?/functional ... QUESTION -> ANSWER -> raises questions -> ACCOUNT -> KNOWLEDGE. This is one of the strongest findings from this book.
b_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Floridi's Network Theory of Account: semantic information answers a question but the answer generates further questions, and relevant information becomes knowledge only when such questions are correctly answered through an appropriate network of informational relations; distinguishes three kinds of 'why' (historical/How-come, teleological/What-for, functional/How-does-it-work, illustrated by Floridi's Berlin and boiling-kettle examples), extending the question taxonomy to what/who/which/where/when/how/why{causal,functional,historical,teleological}/under-what-conditions, formalized as a Question->Answer->raises-questions->Account->Knowledge cycle -- called one of the book's strongest findings.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ANSWER QUALITY: correctness, specificity, completeness, relevance, scope, granularity, evidence, accountability. ... An answer may be correct at LoA-1 but insufficient at LoA-3. ... "The application is slow because the database is overloaded." ... This is exactly the knowledge depth mechanism you were intuitively describing.
b_rows_sample.statement: Replaces the informal 'concreteness of an answer' intuition with eight Answer Quality dimensions (correctness, specificity, completeness, relevance, scope, granularity, evidence, accountability), illustrated by a database-slowness answer chain that is correct at one LoA but requires successive deeper LoAs to fully explain -- identified as exactly the 'knowledge depth' mechanism the project had been intuitively describing.

b_rows_sample.anchor: relevant semantic information becomes knowledge iff it is correctly accounted for. ... truthful + relevant information can still be epistemically lucky. The missing piece is the account connecting the information appropriately to its supporting informational sources. ... remarkably close to what we have been developing in KnowledgeOS around evidence, provenance, verification, justification, observations, deterministic assurance, architectural decisions.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the file's crucial insight: knowledge is not just truth -- truthful and relevant information can still be 'epistemically lucky' without an account connecting it to its supporting informational sources; identifies this account requirement as remarkably close to the project's existing evidence, provenance, verification, justification, observations, deterministic assurance, and architectural-decision work.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CLAIM "Berlin is the capital of Germany" ├── expression (sentence) ├── meaning (proposition) ├── context ├── LoA ├── truth ├── relevance ├── evidence ├── account └── temporal validity ... much closer to KnowledgeOS.
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts a normal knowledge-graph triple (Berlin--capitalOf-->Germany) with a fully-specified KnowledgeOS CLAIM object for the same fact, carrying nine branches (expression/sentence, meaning/proposition, context, LoA, truth, relevance, evidence, account, temporal validity), presented as much closer to what KnowledgeOS should represent.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the UTI challenge: Is a grand unified theory of information possible? He leans toward a non-reductionist position, where different information concepts may be logically interdependent but mutually irreducible. ... We should NOT attempt to put everything into the Kernel. ... The Kernel should define what must be true of a Knowledge Space, not contain the world's knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports Floridi's non-reductionist stance on the Unified Theory of Information challenge (information concepts may be interdependent but mutually irreducible), warning against a KnowledgeKernel containing all ontology/semantics/epistemology/logic/language/domain-knowledge/reasoning; proposes instead a minimal-invariants Kernel (semantics/epistemics/structure) surrounded by extensible spaces (domain space/methodology/governance) -- the Kernel defines what must be true of a Knowledge Space, not the world's knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Keep: A. Level of Abstraction -- Strong Kernel candidate. B. Observable -- Strong candidate. C. Behaviour/constraints -- Strong candidate. D. Semantic information -- Strong candidate. E. Truthfulness -- Kernel-level concern, not a single Boolean. F. Relevance -- Strong candidate, contextual. G. Question->Answer->Account -- Extremely strong candidate. H. Network of information flow -- Strong candidate. I. Structural objects + relations -- Strong candidate. ... Do NOT directly adopt: Reality = information; "Humans are the only known semantic engines"; Floridi's exact epistemological definition of knowledge (treat as research evidence, not constitutional definition).
b_rows_sample.statement: Runs a systematic Zero-Lens keep/reject pass over Floridi's own concepts: nine concepts rated strong-to-extremely-strong Kernel candidates (Level of Abstraction, Observable, Behaviour/constraints, Semantic information, Truthfulness, Relevance, Question->Answer->Account, Network of information flow, Structural objects+relations), versus three items explicitly not to adopt (the metaphysical claim Reality=information, 'humans are the only known semantic engines', and Floridi's exact epistemological knowledge-definition, kept only as research evidence).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 1. Representation boundary ... 2. Semantic boundary ... 3. Epistemic boundary ... 4. Abstraction boundary ... That is a much better definition of the Knowledge Space boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes four Knowledge Space boundary types: Representation (which language/symbols -- word/sentence/document/diagram/code), Semantic (what an expression means -- concept/proposition/reference/predicate/relation), Epistemic (what is actually known -- truth/evidence/relevance/account/confidence/uncertainty), and Abstraction (which part/aspect of the system is modeled -- scope/LoA/purpose/context/observables/behaviour), stated as a much better definition than a single undifferentiated 'boundary'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 1. ENTITY/SYSTEM 2. IDENTITY 3. RELATION 4. OBSERVABLE 5. LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION 6. CONTEXT 7. PURPOSE 8. PROPOSITION/CLAIM 9. QUESTION 10. ANSWER 11. EVIDENCE 12. TRUTH/CORRECTNESS 13. RELEVANCE 14. ACCOUNT 15. TEMPORALITY 16. PROVENANCE 17. CONSTRAINT/BEHAVIOUR ... WORD, SENTENCE, DOCUMENT, TOPIC, ARTICLE, BOOK, MANIFESTO, CONSTITUTION would not necessarily be Kernel primitives.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a 17-item candidate Kernel list (Entity/System, Identity, Relation, Observable, Level of Abstraction, Context, Purpose, Proposition/Claim, Question, Answer, Evidence, Truth/Correctness, Relevance, Account, Temporality, Provenance, Constraint/Behaviour) explicitly excluding Word, Sentence, Document, Topic, Article, Book, Manifesto, and Constitution as representational/organizational structures built on top of the Kernel -- a major architectural simplification.

b_rows_sample.anchor: information can be approached through different spaces: probability space, modal space, state space, inference space, and data space. ... Perhaps Knowledge Space is a structured family of interrelated spaces ... Levels of Abstraction provide the coordinate system/interface through which these spaces can be related. That is, in my view, the most valuable result of reading this book.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the file's most valuable result: Knowledge Space is not one mathematical space but a structured family of interrelated spaces (Data Space: symbols/expressions/documents; Semantic Space: propositions/meanings/references; Epistemic Space: knowledge/evidence/beliefs; State Space: dynamics/change; Modal Space: possible states; Inference Space: reasoning paths), with Levels of Abstraction functioning as the coordinate system/interface relating them.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Floridi does not give us the final KnowledgeOS Kernel. ... stop asking: "What things belong inside KnowledgeOS?" and start asking: "What structures and transformations are invariant when knowledge is represented, abstracted, questioned, verified, related, and accounted for?" ... Knowledge Space Model v0.2 ... test it against the next book—especially Williamson.
b_rows_sample.statement: Declines to freeze the Kernel after Floridi, reframing the guiding question from 'what things belong inside KnowledgeOS?' to 'what structures and transformations are invariant when knowledge is represented, abstracted, questioned, verified, related, and accounted for?', naming the current state 'Knowledge Space Model v0.2' and committing to test it next against Williamson, since Floridi's biggest unresolved assumption (identified explicitly) is what makes semantic information become knowledge -- relevance and account.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Dretske instead develops: information -> information-caused belief -> knowledge. He explicitly proposes an information-theoretic replacement for the traditional justified-true-belief account. ... a particularly subtle distinction between information causing a belief and information causally sustaining a belief. ... OBSERVATION -> INFORMATION ACQUISITION -> BELIEF FORMATION -> BELIEF SUSTENANCE -> KNOWLEDGE CLAIM.
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts Floridi's semantic-information->relevance->account->knowledge route with Dretske's information->information-caused-belief->knowledge route (an information-theoretic replacement for justified-true-belief), distinguishing information causing a belief from information causally sustaining it, proposing a five-stage pipeline Observation->Information Acquisition->Belief Formation->Belief Sustenance->Knowledge Claim instead of treating evidence as a static attachment to a claim.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Floridi and Dretske are converging on some things but disagreeing or emphasizing different layers on others. That is precisely what we need from the Zero Lens. ... I would not freeze the Kernel yet. The next useful step is to construct a Floridi × Dretske comparative matrix and derive only the invariants that survive both books.
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes Floridi and Dretske converge on some points and diverge/emphasize different layers on others, which is exactly the intended use of the Zero Lens; explicitly declines to freeze the Kernel, proposing a Floridi x Dretske comparative matrix to derive only the invariants surviving both books as the next research step.

b_rows_sample.anchor: When should a database answer "I don't know" to a query? ... question answering itself is epistemic behavior. ... ANSWERABILITY, INFORMATION SUFFICIENCY, KNOWLEDGE, COMPUTABILITY, CONFIDENCE, COMPLETENESS. Those are not the same quantity.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses Fagin et al.'s database 'when should I-don't-know be returned?' question to argue question-answering is itself epistemic behavior (Question->Knowledge regime->{enough information? awareness? computation? evidence? shared knowledge?}->YES/NO/UNKNOWN), extending Floridi's Answer Quality dimensions by separating Answerability, Information Sufficiency, Knowledge, Computability, Confidence, and Completeness as non-identical quantities.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is moving in an infinite Knowledge Space. ... Knowledge should serve the nature of the Knowledge Space itself. ... Knowledge is not merely accumulated inside the Knowledge Space; its structure, relations, boundaries, changes, and representations should remain coherent with the nature of the space being modelled.
b_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates sixteen prior project intuitions about Knowledge Space (infinite, boundary-crossing, facts+arguments, dynamic, representation≠knowledge, LoA-dependent, tolerates uncertainty/contradiction/suspension, changes via expansion/revision/contraction, entrenchment-dependent importance, exceeds language, questions open paths, explanations reduce surprise) into one closing principle: knowledge's structure/relations/boundaries/changes/representations must remain coherent with the nature of the space being modeled, not merely accumulate inside it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Yes — with partial operations and explicit epistemic types. The word partial is crucial
a_rows_sample.statement: States that KnowledgeOS can be a formal composable/revisable system precisely because operations are partial, allowing 'operation undefined' rather than invented results.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Observe:W\rightarrow\mathcal O ... Infer:\mathcal E\rightharpoonup\mathcal A ... Validate:\mathcal A\times\mathcal E\rightarrow\mathcal V
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines eight typed operations between universe subsets, several explicitly partial.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Infer(E)=\bot ... \bot\neq False. And \bot\neq Unknown ... no justified result exists under the specified inference system
a_rows_sample.statement: States a total Infer would encourage hallucination on insufficient evidence, defining bottom as a distinct non-result: bottom≠False, bottom≠Unknown.

a_rows_sample.anchor: False: H=False ... Unknown: Unknown(H) ... Undefined: f(x)=\bot ... False\neq Unknown\neq Undefined
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally distinguishes three failure states as mathematically distinct: False, Unknown, and Undefined.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Hypothesis, SupportedClaim, ValidatedClaim, Forecast, DecisionCandidate, AuthorizedAction ... These are not simply statuses. They determine what operations are permitted
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces epistemic types that determine, not merely describe, which operations are permitted.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Promote:Hypothesis\times Evidence\rightharpoonup SupportedClaim ... a hypothesis does not automatically become supported merely because an LLM produced it
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an admissible type-promotion operation from Hypothesis to SupportedClaim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Hypothesis\notin Domain(Execute) ... EpistemicTypeError. This is the epistemic equivalent of a programming type error
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines epistemic type safety via domain membership, giving EpistemicTypeError.

a_rows_sample.anchor: World\rightarrow Knowledge\rightarrow Action\rightarrow World ... OperationalCycle from EpistemicCircularity
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes a legitimate operational cycle from problematic epistemic circularity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: g\circ f only when Range(f)\subseteq Domain(g) ... SemanticTypeCompatibility is a precondition for composition
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines composition validity and the epistemic composition law of semantic type compatibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: RiskModel\circ Infer is not a valid composition ... Evidence\rightarrow Inference\rightarrow Validation\rightarrow Model\rightarrow Decision ... rather than Evidence\rightarrow LLM\rightarrow Decision ... a major architectural strengthening
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing an invalid composition requires an intervening Validate step, giving a stronger assurance path than direct LLM-to-decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: id_X(x)=x ... identity element for composition
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an identity transformation giving the algebra an identity element.

a_rows_sample.anchor: h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f ... PureTransformation from StateTransition
a_rows_sample.statement: States expected associativity for pure composition while requiring PureTransformation to be distinguished from StateTransition, worked with unit-conversion vs ApproveChange examples.

a_rows_sample.anchor: (\mathcal K,\circ,\oplus,\ldots) algebra of knowledge objects ... (K_t,event)\rightarrow K_{t+1} algebra of state transitions ... should not be conflated
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes two distinct mathematical layers that should not be conflated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge:K\times K\rightharpoonup K' ... Clean merge K_1\oplus K_2=K_3 ... Merge with conflict K_3+ConflictSet ... Unmergeable Merge=\bot
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines partial knowledge merge with three possible outcomes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_1\preceq K_2 ... must not mean K_2 is more correct. It means K_2 contains at least as much represented information ... MoreInformation\neq MoreTruth
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an information ordering explicitly distinct from a truth ordering.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_1\sqsubseteq K_2 refinement (adds information without violating K_1's semantics) ... K_1\xrightarrow{E}K_2 revision (previous commitments may be defeated)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines knowledge refinement distinct from revision.

b_rows_sample.statement: Three amendments: (1) the 'nine kinds' are held as candidate archetypes, not frozen primitives, until MM-1 resolves whether KIND is itself a dimension; (2) CONTAINER is demoted from CONFIRMED to CANDIDATE, since its distinguishing edge ('generates Projections') is observed in only one space (the EKP) and nesting is unevidenced (H-3); (3) PURPOSE is flagged for its own investigation (U-MM-4, waits on D-5).

b_rows_sample.statement: Three additional kinds were repeatedly found by the passes but missing from the A-G candidate list: PURPOSE (mission/vision, found twice in the Relationship Ontology), CONTAINER (Knowledge Space — declared boundary, nesting), and PROJECTION (derived, operating in production).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Classification — every gap from the projection ... G-1..G-5
b_rows_sample.statement: Five gaps classified by category (Structural/Behavioral/Evolutionary) and cause: G-1 (I-4/ATTESTS/PROJECTION inert-vs-attested) is EVOLUTIONARY, caused by a missing lifecycle, belongs to LIFECYCLE. G-2 (SPECIALIZES, Engineering Knowledge -> product knowledge) is EVOLUTIONARY, a missing relationship, belongs to ONTOLOGY. G-3 (external authority/CONSTRAINS) is BEHAVIORAL, a missing relationship (obligation != ownership), belongs to GOVERNANCE. G-4 (PRODUCT vs DEPLOYMENT/INSTANTIATES) is STRUCTURAL but dissolves: a deployment is a nested Knowledge Space, so it belongs to ONTOLOGY as resolved, no new concept. G-5 (Runtime Adapter disappeared in both new domains) is STRUCTURAL but is a confirmation of Hexagonal behaving correctly, not a failure.

b_rows_sample.statement: H-3 (the nesting question) is answered by G-4: Knowledge Spaces nest, and a deployment is the nested case. No new concept was introduced; the ontology already explained the evidence, which is the test the commission set.
